tip: For past regrets, pair 'tivesse' plus the '-do' form ('começado') with 'teria' plus the '-do' form ('terminado'): if I had, I would have.
'A gente' means we in casual speech but takes singular verbs, so 'tivesse' and 'plantaria', never the 'nós' forms.
'Se fala' means 'is spoken'; the 'se' makes the verb passive with no separate word for 'is': 'aqui se fala'.
'Lhe' means to him or to her: 'eu lhe dei o recado' = I gave the message to him or her.
In the passive, the '-do' form agrees with the subject: 'casa' is feminine, so 'reformada', not 'reformado'.
Before an infinitive, 'é proibido' doesn't change: 'é proibido fumar'. It agrees only when a noun follows, as in 'proibida a entrada'.
'Tampouco' means not either, the negative of 'também'. 'Tampouco ele sabia' = he did not know either. It is a touch more formal than 'também não'.
In the passive, the doer follows 'por', which contracts with 'a' to 'pela': 'foi paga pela empresa' = was paid by the company.
For an unreal present situation, use 'se' plus the past subjunctive ('fosse'), then the conditional: 'se ele não fosse orgulhoso, pediria desculpas'.
Recommendation verbs take the past subjunctive: 'recomendou que tomasse', where English just says 'he drink'.
'Embora', meaning although, always takes the subjunctive: 'embora esteja frio', never 'embora está frio'.
'Disse que' is the standard way to report speech; casual Brazilian talk often swaps in 'falou que'.
'Quanto mais... mais' means 'the more... the more', as in 'quanto mais estudo, mais percebo'.
'Aluga-se' uses passive 'se', so the verb agrees with its noun; the plural would be 'alugam-se salas'.
'Parar de' plus a verb means to stop doing it: the command 'pare de fazer barulho' = stop making noise.
'Apesar de' means despite and is followed by an infinitive, as in 'apesar de estar doente'.
'Deixar de' plus a verb means to stop or quit doing it: 'deixou de fumar' = she quit smoking.
'Acabar de' plus an infinitive means to have just done something: 'acabei de ler' = I just read.
'Assim que', meaning as soon as, takes the future subjunctive: 'assim que eu chegar' = as soon as I arrive.
'Andar' plus the '-ndo' form describes a recent ongoing habit: 'anda comendo' = she's been eating lately.
'Diz-se que' means 'it is said that', a way to report rumor without saying who: 'diz-se que ele vai se candidatar'.
'Até onde eu sei' means as far as I know; use it to hedge a statement, as in 'até onde eu sei, o projeto foi aprovado'.
'Uma vez que' looks like 'one time that' but means 'once' or 'given that'; it isn't counting times.
'Desde que' can mean 'since' (time) or 'as long as' (condition).
'Acabar de' plus an infinitive means to have just done something. 'Acabamos de receber' = we have just received, a very recent past.
'Andar' plus the '-ndo' form describes a recent ongoing tendency. 'Eles andam brigando' = they have been fighting lately, not literally walking.
'Deixar de' plus an infinitive means to stop or give up doing something. 'Deixei de tentar' = I stopped trying.
'À medida que' is the proportional 'as', the more X the more Y; it isn't the 'like' meaning of 'como'.
'Tornar a' plus a verb means to do it again: 'tornou a ligar' = he called again. It's a bit formal.
'Ou seja' is literally 'or be it', with 'seja' the subjunctive of 'ser', frozen into the phrase 'in other words'.
